answer:
REGULATORY BRIEF - INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (IA) QUALIFICATIONS FOR MAJOR ALTERATIONS
Jurisdiction: U.S. 14 CFR, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 65, Subpart D (Mechanics), read with Part 43 and 14 CFR 1.1.
Primary controlling provision (the answer to the ask): 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1) through (5). Supporting: 65.93 (currency/renewal), 65.95(a)(1) (the major-repair/major-alteration privilege), 65.95(b) (limitations, paraphrazed - see verification checklist), 14 CFR 1.1 (definition of major alteration), Part 43 Subpart A (43.5, repairs and alterations: general).

=== PART A - QUALIFICATIONS TO HOLD AN IA (14 CFR 65.91(c), QUOTED VERBATIM) ===
The applicant must satisfy all five conditions; they are conjunctive, not alternative.

'(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must-
(1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
(2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
(3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
(4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
(5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.'
[Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-65.91 - fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:03Z, sha256 8dd2b52b76db]

Engineering translation of each condition (what an applicant must actually be able to document):
(1) Mechanic certificate currency - A + P, both ratings currently effective, both in effect a total of at least 3 years. An airframe-only or powerplant-only certificate does not qualifiy.
(2) Engagement - at least 2 years immediately preceding application spent maintaining aircraft certificated/maintained under the CFR (this is the 'actively engaged' test, not merely 'employed in aviation').
(3) Fixed base of operations - a location where the applicant can be reached in person or by telephone during a normal working week; it need not be the place where IA authority is exercised.
(4) Facility/data qualificaiton - equipment, facilities, and inspection data sufficient to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, and related parts/appliances. This is the provision that makes the IA holder's shop/library part of the qualificaiton, not an afterthought.
(5) Written test - the test is specifically oriented to returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and after annual and progressive inspections under Part 43. Note this is the eligibility test; it is distinct from the oral test in 65.93(c).

Application mechanics (65.91(a)-(b)): application is made on the form and in the manner prescribed by the FAA, and eligibility is verified before the written test is administred. Paraphrazed here; confirm exact wording at eCFR 65.91(a)-(b) before quoting in a compliance document.

=== PART B - CONDITIONS FOR EXERCISING IA PRIVILEGES ON MAJOR ALTERATIONS (14 CFR 65.95(a)(1), QUOTED VERBATIM) ===
'(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may-
(1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and'
[Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95 - fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:03Z, sha256 04eedc455339]

Three operative gates for a major alteration, all of which must be satisfied at the moment of approval:
Gate 1 - Scope: aircraft or related part/appliance, excluding aircraft maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121. On a Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft the IA does not hold this approval authority.
Gate 2 - Part 43 compliance: the alteration must have been accomplished in accordance with Part 43.
Gate 3 - Technical data: 'the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.' This is the gate that most often fails an IA approval. The IA's signature approves for RETURN TO SERVICE; it does not approve the design/alteration data itself. Approving a major alteration accomplished on unapproved or applicant-generated data is outside the privilege even if the workmanship is impeccable.

=== PART C - CURRENCY / CONTINUING QUALIFICATIONS (14 CFR 65.93, QUOTED VERBATIM WHERE RETRIEVED) ===
'(a) Each inspection authorization expires on March 31 of each odd-numbered year. However, the holder may exercise the privileges of that authorization only while he holds a currently effective mechanic certificate with both a currently effective airframe rating and a currently effective powerplant rating.'
[Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65 - fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:10Z, sha256 ba0b5fa97a92]

'(c) An inspection authorization holder who does not complete one of the activities set forth in 65.93(a)(1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period may not exercise inspection authorization privileges after March 31 of the first year. The inspection authorization holder may resume exercising inspection authorization privileges after passing an oral test from an FAA inspector to determine that the applicant's knowledge of the applicable regulations and standards is current. An inspection authorization holder who passes this oral test is deemed to have completed the requirements of 65.93(a)(1) through (5) by March 31 of the first year.'
[Source: http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.93 - fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:09Z, sha256 d50ca977ec87]

Consolidated currency qualificaiton for exercising IA privileges (including on major alterations):
C1. Currently effective mechanic certificate, both airframe and powerplant ratings currently effective (65.93(a), quoted above).
C2. IA within its 2-year period; expiry March 31 of odd-numbered years (65.93(a), quoted above).
C3. At least one of the 65.93(a)(1)-(5) renewal activities completed by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year period; if missed, privileges stop after that date and resume only on passing the FAA oral test (65.93(c), quoted above).
C4. The enumerated content of 65.93(a)(1)-(5) is deliberately NOT reproduced in this deliverable: the retrieved passages did not contain that list verbatim and it is marked unverified in the source set. Confirm it at eCFR 65.93(a) before relying on any particular activity (annual inspections, progressive inspections, major repairs/alterations, airworthiness-directive work, refresher training) as a renewal basis.

=== PART D - WHAT COUNTS AS A MAJOR ALTERATION (14 CFR 1.1, DEFINITION) ===
'Major alteration' means an alteration that might appreciably affect the weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other characteristics affecting airworthiness. This definition is what triggers the Part 43 / 65.95 approval path in the first place; a minor alteration does not require IA approval for return to service under 65.95(a)(1).

=== PART E - OPERATIONAL CHECKLIST AN IA SHOULD BE ABLE TO CLOSE ON A MAJOR ALTERATION ===
1. Qualification: current A+P mechanic certificate in hand (C1).
2. Qualification: IA within its 2-year period and 65.93(a) activity satisfied by March 31 of the first year, or oral-test requalificaiton documented (C2, C3).
3. Scope: aircraft not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program (Gate 1).
4. Data: alteration accomplished on technical data approved by the Administrator - identify the approval basis (e.g., STC, FAA field approval on Form 337, ODA/derived approval) and retain it (Gate 3).
5. Workmanship: inspection performed against that data, with the IA's own inspection data available per 65.91(c)(4).
6. Records: approval for return to service recorded in accordance with Part 43, with the IA's certificate number and the approval basis traceable.
7. Renewal bookkeeping: the 65.93 activity log maintained continuously, not reconstructed at renewal time.

=== PART F - COMMON FAILURE POINTS ===
F1. Confusing the 65.91(c)(5) written test with the 65.93(c) oral test. They are different events serving different purposes (initial eligibility vs. restoration after a missed renewal activity).
F2. Treating the IA as authority to approve the alteration DESIGN. It is authority to approve for RETURN TO SERVICE; the design data must already be Administrator-approved (65.95(a)(1)).
F3. Overlooking the Part 121 continuous-airworthiness exclusion in 65.95(a)(1).
F4. Treating the IA as a lifetime credential. It expires March 31 of odd-numbered years and carries a mid-period activity gate at March 31 of the first year.
F5. Assuming an airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanic qualifys - 65.91(c)(1) requires both.

=== PART G - VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THIS IS USED IN A COMPLIANCE OR TRAINING DOCUMENT ===
V1. 65.91(a)-(b): application form/manner and pre-test eligibility review - paraphrazed here, confirm verbatim.
V2. 65.93(a)(1)-(5): enumerated renewal activities - NOT sourced verbatim; confirm at eCFR 65.93(a).
V3. 65.95(b) and any (c)/(d): limitations - paraphrazed here, confirm verbatim at eCFR 65.95. Do not republish the paraphrase as regulation text.
V4. 43.5 (repairs and alterations: general) - cited as the Part 43 technical-data rule; confirm section number and wording.
V5. Part 43 record/Form 337 requirement for major repairs and major alterations - section number not asserted here; confirm in Part 43 Subpart A before citing.

=== PART H - SOURCES ===
S1. 14 CFR 65.91 - https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-65.91 (fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:03Z, sha256 8dd2b52b76db)
S2. 14 CFR 65.95 - https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95 (fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:03Z, sha256 04eedc455339)
S3. 14 CFR 65.93 - http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.93 (fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:09Z, sha256 d50ca977ec87)
S4. 14 CFR Part 65 (expiry/currency text) - https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65 (fetched 2026-11-15T03:41:10Z, sha256 ba0b5fa97a92)
S5. FAA Inspection Authorization Information Guide - https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/ia_info_guide.pdf (guidance; non-binding, useful for the operational checklist in Part E)
S6. GovInfo PDF of 65.91 (CFR 2025 title 14 vol 2) - https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title14-vol2/pdf/CFR-2025-title14-vol2-sec65-91.pdf

=== BOTTOM LINE (ONE SENTENCE) ===
To hold and exercise an inspection authorization for major alterations you must meet all five 65.91(c) qualificaitons (current A+P mechanic certificate held 3 years total, 2 years of active engagement, fixed base of operations, equipment/facilities/inspection data, and the written test), remain current under 65.93 (expiry March 31 of odd-numbered years, mid-period activity gate with oral-test restoration), and approve the alteration only where it is within Part 43 and was accomplished on technical data approved by the Administrator, excluding Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft (65.95(a)(1)).

question: IA
answer:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — QUALIFICATIONS FOR INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (IA) WITH RESPECT TO MAJOR ALTERATIONS, 14 CFR / FAA-AMT

0. HOW I READ THE QUESTION (disclosed interpretation)
The question 'what are the qualifications for inspection auth regaurding major alterations' has two distinct regulatory senses, and the answer is different in each. Both are answered below:
  Sense A — QUALIFICATIONS TO BE ISSUED AN IA. What a mechanic must show the FAA before an inspection authorization is issued. Governed by 14 CFR 65.91.
  Sense B — WHAT THE IA IS QUALIFIED/AUTHORIZED TO DO about a major alteration once held. Governed by the inspection-authorization privileges paragraph of 14 CFR part 65 subpart D (cited here as 65.95) plus part 43.
The link between them is explicit in the regulation: the IA written test in 65.91(c)(5) is by its own terms a test on returning aircraft to service 'after major repairs and major alterations', so major alterations are baked into the qualification itself, not merely into the later privilege.
Note on 'FAA-AMT': read as FAA aviation maintenance technician context (i.e., the Part 65 mechanic/IA framework). If the token is a specific course, exam-bank or credential code, that mapping is not verifiable from the grounding; the regulatory answer below does not depend on it.

1. GOVERNING TEXT MAP
| Layer | Cite | What it supplies |
| Definition | 14 CFR 1.1 | What counts as a 'major alteration' (this is the trigger for everything else) |
| Return to service / records | 14 CFR part 43 (see 43.5 return-to-service approval; part 43 records, incl. FAA Form 337 for major repairs and alterations) | Who may approve, and what must be recorded |
| IA eligibility | 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1)-(5) | The five qualifications to BE ISSUED an IA |
| IA duration/currency | 14 CFR 65.92 / 65.93 (verify numbering) | That the IA must be currently effective at the moment of approval |
| IA privilege re major alterations | 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) (verify section number) | Inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration |
Note: subpart D does NOT create a separate 'major alteration rating' or endorsement. There is one IA credential; its scope is defined by the privileges text, not by a rating on the certificate.

2. SENSE A — THE FIVE QUALIFICATIONS TO BE ISSUED AN IA (14 CFR 65.91(c))
Regulatory text (as fetched): '(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must— (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years; (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter; (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority; (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.'

| # | Qualification | Threshold / condition (exact) | Evidence a compliance reviewer should see |
| 1 | Mechanic certificate with BOTH airframe and powerplant ratings | Each rating currently effective AND in effect for a total of at least 3 years | FAA mechanic certificate showing both ratings; airman records |
| 2 | Actively engaged in maintaining aircraft | At least the 2-year period before the application date, maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with the chapter | Employment / work-order / logbook history covering the full 2 years |
| 3 | Fixed base of operations | Locatable in person or by telephone during a normal working week; need NOT be where the authority is exercised | Address + telephone on the application |
| 4 | Equipment, facilities, inspection data | Available and sufficient to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | Tool list; current maintenance manuals, ADs, and inspection data subscriptions |
| 5 | Written test | Pass a written test on ability to inspect per safety standards for return to service after major repairs AND major alterations, and annual and progressive inspections under part 43 | FAA test result / airman record |
Two structural points that answer the question directly:
  - A mechanic holding only one rating (airframe-only or powerplant-only) cannot qualify. Both are required.
  - Qualification #5 is not a generic airworthiness test. Its published scope is expressly return-to-service after MAJOR REPAIRS and MAJOR ALTERATIONS, plus annual and progressive inspections under part 43. That is the sense in which 'major alterations' is a qualification topic rather than only a privilege topic.

3. SENSE B — WHAT THE IA IS QUALIFIED TO DO ABOUT A MAJOR ALTERATION (14 CFR 65.95(a)(1))
Regulatory text (as fetched): '(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may— (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; ...'
Converted to a four-condition test. ALL four must be true before an IA may sign:
| Cond. | Condition | Fail consequence |
| C1 | The article is an aircraft or a related part or appliance | Outside the privilege |
| C2 | The work was a MAJOR repair or MAJOR alteration (see 4 below) | If minor, the IA privilege is not the operative authority; routine part 43 sign-off by the performing mechanic applies |
| C3 | The work was done in accordance with technical data APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATOR | IA may NOT approve for return to service; escalate to the data holder / design-approval path |
| C4 | The aircraft is NOT maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 | IA may NOT approve; approval must come through the operator's approved part 121 program |
Plus a standing precondition: the individual's IA must be currently effective on the date of approval (duration/currency, see 6 below).
Three scope limits worth stating plainly to any AMT audiance:
  - The IA privilege is a RETURN-TO-SERVICE APPROVAL, not a design-approval authority. An IA cannot create, extend or 'field-approve' alteration data. If the technical data is not Administrator-approved, the IA is not the path.
  - The IA privilege does not authorize PERFORMING the alteration; performance is governed by part 43 and the mechanic/repairman certificate. The IA function is inspection and approoval for return to service.
  - The part 121 exclusion is airframe-level: it turns on how the aircraft is maintained, not on who does the work.

4. THE TRIGGER — DEFINITION OF 'MAJOR ALTERATION' (14 CFR 1.1)
Regulatory text (as fetched): '*Major alteration* means an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propellers specifications— (1) That might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) That is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.'
Apply it as: GATEWAY (not listed in the aircraft/engine/propeller specifications) AND then EITHER prong:
  Prong 1 — six named qualities plus a catch-all: (i) weight, (ii) balance, (iii) structural strength, (iv) performance, (v) powerplant operation, (vi) flight characteristics, or (vii) other qualities affecting airworthiness. The test is 'MIGHT APPRECIABLY AFFECT' — a possibility threshold, not a demonstrated-effect threshold. Do not require proof of actual effect.
  Prong 2 — not done according to accepted practices, OR cannot be done by elementary operations.
Because the prongs are joined by 'or', satisfying either one suffices. A classification worksheet should record which prong was relied on and the specific quality implicated.

5. CONBINED DECISION PROCEDURE (apply in order; each step is a go/no-go)
1. Is the individual's IA currently effective today (duration + currency)? If no -> STOP; no IA privilege exists.
2. Is the article an aircraft or related part/appliance? If no -> outside 65.95(a)(1).
3. Classify the work against 1.1 (gateway + prong 1 or prong 2). Record the classification and the basis.
   - Minor alteration -> the IA privilege is not needed; part 43 records/sign-off by the performing mechanic.
   - Major alteration -> continue.
4. Is the aircraft maintained under a part 121 continuous airworthiness program? If yes -> STOP; IA cannot approve; route to the operator's approved program.
5. Was the work performed in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator? If no -> STOP; IA cannot approve; the data must first be approved (or the alteration re-scoped to fit approved data). If yes -> continue.
6. Was the work performed in accordance with part 43? If no -> do not approve; document the finding.
7. Inspect per the applicable approved data and the IA's inspection-data set (65.91(c)(4) obligation continues in force after issuance). If airworthy -> approve for return to service and make the required records (major repair/alteration record on FAA Form 337, plus the part 43 maintenance record entry signed by the IA). If not -> do not approve; record the discrepancy.

6. DURATION / CURRENCY OF THE IA (verify before reliance)
An otherwise-qualified individual loses the privilege the moment the authorization lapses. Subpart D time-limits and renews the IA and imposes a currency condition (commonly cited as 65.92 currency and 65.93 duration, on a fixed cycle tied to March 31 of odd-numbered years, with a 90-day pre-expiration activity condition). Confirm the exact section numbers and the current cycle against eCFR before quoting them in a filing; they are not part of the fetched text I am relying on for the five eligibility elements.

7. COMMON NON-QUALIFICATIONS / ERORS THIS ANSWER IS MEANT TO PREVENT
  - Treating an A&P mechanic as able to approve a major alteration for return to service without an IA. The mechanic may PERFORM; the approoval requires the IA (or another authorized approver).
  - Approving an alteration whose technical data is not Administrator-approved.
  - Approving for return to service on a part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft.
  - Mis-classifying a major alteration as minor (or the reverse) by skipping the 1.1 gateway or by demanding proof of actual airworthiness effect instead of 'might appreciably affect'.
  - Signing off on an expired or non-current IA.
  - Omitting the major repair/alteration record (Form 337) or the part 43 record entry.
  - Reading the IA as authority to approv the DESIGN of an alteration.

8. VERIFY-BEFORE-RELIANCE LIST (honest limits of this answer)
  - Paragraph lettering of 65.91 is reproduced as '(c)' from the fetched eCFR text; confirm the lettering on the live page before quoting in a regulatory filing.
  - The privileges provision is cited as 65.95 per subpart D; the fetched quote came from the subpart D page rather than a section-specific page — confirm the section number.
  - 65.92/65.93 duration and currency details are flagged, not asserted.
  - Part 43 section numbers (return-to-service approoval; record entries) are cited by function; confirm numbering before formal citation.
  - The part 121 exclusion is quoted as fetched; confirm no later amendment has added other continuous-airworthiness programs (e.g., part 135) to the exclusion.
  - Current text only; no historical-version analysis is supplied.

9. SOURCES (as fetched, current eCFR)
  - 14 CFR 65.91 — http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.91 (fetched 2026-11-15T03:43:02Z, sha256 8dd2b52b76db)
  - 14 CFR part 65 subpart D (privileges) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D (fetched 2026-11-15T03:43:02Z, sha256 1dc594967131)
  - 14 CFR 1.1 (definitions) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1 (fetched 2026-11-15T03:43:02Z, sha256 2b43d8c55cce)
  - Cross-check: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/65.91 ; https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title14-vol2/pdf/CFR-2025-title14-vol2-sec65-92.pdf

BOTTOM LINE. Qualifations for an IA regarding major alterations = the five 65.91(c) eligibility elements (both ratings in effect at least 3 years; at least 2 years actively engaged; fixed base of operations; equipment/facilities/inspection data; and a written test whose published scope is return to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual/progressive inspections under part 43). Once held, the major-alteration authority is the 65.95(a)(1) privilege, conditional on Administrator-approved technical data, part 43 compliance, and the aircraft not being maintained under a part 121 continuous-airworthiness program — with the alteration classified as major under 14 CFR 1.1 in the first place.

question: IA
answer:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) and Major Alterations — Qualification Requirements

Governing law: 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart E (Inspection Authorization), sections 65.91 through 65.95, cross-referenced to 14 CFR Part 43 (Appendix A, Major Alterations; Appendix B, Recording of Major Repairs and Major Alterations). All regulatory text below is verbatim from eCFR as fetched 2026-11-15T03:45:08Z (sha256 digests recorded in the source list).

Citation correction to the research package: the package labeled sections 65.91 and 65.95 as 'Subpart D' and 65.93 as 'Subpart E'. In 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D is Mechanics (roughly 65.71-65.83) and Subpart E is Inspection Authorization (65.91-65.95). All three sections at issue are Subpart E. The section numbers and quoted text are unaffected; only the subpart label is corrected here, and the corrected URLs appear in the source list.

## 1. Answer in one paragraph

There are three distinct sets of qualifications bearing on major alterations, and they must not be mixed:

(a) Qualifications to obtain the IA at all — 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1)-(5). Only subparagraph (c)(5) is major-alteration-specific: a written test on the ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations (and annual and progressive inspections under Part 43). Subparagraphs (c)(1)-(4) are generic mechanic-authorization qualifications.

(b) The scope condition built into the IA privilege itself for major alterations — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1). The IA holder may inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration only if (i) the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator, (ii) the action is taken in accordance with Part 43, and (iii) the aircraft is not maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121.

(c) Requalification — 14 CFR 65.93. Renewal for a 2-year period requires March-of-odd-numbered-year evidence at the responsible Flight Standards office that the applicant still meets 65.91(c)(1)-(4), plus completion of one listed activity in each year of the 2-year cycle. One of those activities is directly major-alteration-based: at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days the current authority was held (65.93(a)(2)).

## 2. Table 1 — Initial eligibility to hold an IA (14 CFR 65.91(c))

| Element | Requirement | Regulatory text | Practitioner evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| (c)(1) | Mechanic certificate, airframe and powerplant ratings, currently effective, in effect a total of at least 3 years | > Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years; | Certificate with both ratings; 'total of at least 3 years' is cumulative time in effect, not necessarily continuous. |
| (c)(2) | Recent active engagement | > Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter; | 2-year lookback immediately before application; work must be on aircraft within the scope of the chapter. |
| (c)(3) | Fixed base of operations | > Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority; | Fixed base need not be where the IA authority is exercised — do not impose a location restriction the rule does not contain. |
| (c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, inspection data | > Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; | This is the provision that makes major-alteration approval possible: the IA must be able to reach the Administrator-approved technical data against which conformity is judged. |
| (c)(5) | Written test | > Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter. | The only eligibility element whose subject matter is expressly major alterations and major repairs. |

## 3. Table 2 — Condition on the major-alteration privilege (14 CFR 65.95(a)(1))

> (a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and

Decomposed into five testable conditions:

| # | Condition | What fails the test |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The person holds a currently effective inspection authorization | Expired or un-renewned IA (see Table 3). |
| 2 | The article is an aircraft or related part or appliance that has undergone a major repair or major alteration | Work that is not major under Appendix A to Part 43; ordinary maintenance does not require IA approval. |
| 3 | The aircraft is not maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121 | Any Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft — excluded by the parenthetical, regardless of data quality. |
| 4 | The work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator | Alteration accomplished on unapproved or owner-generated data that lacks FAA approval. |
| 5 | The approval is made in accordance with Part 43 | Procedural non-compliance with Part 43 (inspection, return-to-service, and recording requirements). |

Note: 65.95(a) also contains a second privilege (annual and progressive inspections) not at issue here, and 65.95(b) contains further limitations on exercising IA privileges. The full current text of 65.95(b) was not captured in the research package — see section 8.

## 4. Table 3 — Requalification / renewal (14 CFR 65.93)

> (a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, to be eligible for renewal of an inspection authorization for a 2-year period an applicant must present evidence during the month of March of each odd-numbered year, at the responsible Flight Standards office, that the applicant still meets the requirements of 65.91(c)(1) through (4).
> In addition, during the time the applicant held the inspection authorization, the applicant must show completion of one of the activities in paragraphs (a)(1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period, and completion of one of the five activities during the second year of the 2-year period:
> (1) Performed at least one annual inspection for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or
> (2) Performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or
> (3) Performed or supervised and approved at least one progressive inspection in accordance with standards prescribed by the Administrator; or
> (4) Attended and successfully completed a refresher course, acceptable to the Administrator, of not less than 8 hours of instruction; or
> (5) Passed an oral test by an FAA inspector to determine that the applicant's knowledge of applicable regulations and standards is current.

Structural points a practitioner must not miss:
- The March window falls in each odd-numbered year (…, 2025, 2027, 2029, …). With the text as fetched on 2026-11-15, the next renewal window is March 2027.
- Two separate activity completions are required: one by March 31 of the first year, one during the second year. A single activity should not be assumed to satisfy both.
- The written test of 65.91(c)(5) is not re-administered at renewal; currency of knowledge is instead evidenced through options (4) or (5), or through the work-volume options (1)-(3).
- Option (a)(2) is the direct major-alteration currency route and is the provision most often confused with 65.95(a)(1). 65.93(a)(2) is a renewal-credit rule about how many major repairs/alterations the IA performed; it is not a privilege and confers no approval authority.

## 5. Practitioner decision procedure — may this IA approve this major alteration?

1. Characterize the work. Determine whether the alteration is major under Appendix A to Part 43. If it is not major, no IA approval is required; the work is returned to service under ordinary mechanic privileges and Part 43.
2. Check the data. Confirm the alteration was accomplished in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator (e.g., type certificate data sheet, supplemental type certificate, or other FAA-approved data). If the data is not approved, stop — 65.95(a)(1) is not satisfied and no IA may approve the article for return to service.
3. Check the aircraft's maintenance program. If the aircraft is maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121, stop — the parenthetical in 65.95(a)(1) excludes it; route to the operator's approved program and authorizer representative.
4. Check IA currency. Confirm the individual's inspection authorization is currently effective for the present 2-year period (renewed in March of the odd-numbered year). An expired authorization supports no approval.
5. Check the practical support. Confirm the 65.91(c)(3)-(4) support still exists — access to the approved data, equipment and facilities needed to compare the alteration against that data. This is what makes the conformity judgement in step 2 possible rather than nominal.
6. Inspect and approve. Perform the inspection in accordance with Part 43 and approve for return to service only if conformity to the approved data is established. Record the major alteration as required by Appendix B to Part 43 (FAA Form 337 recording of major repairs and major alterations).
7. If any of steps 1-5 fails, do not approve. The article remains unapproved until a person with the requisite authority acts; a mechanic's ordinary privileges do not extend to approving a major alteration for return to service.
8. Document. Record the approved-data reference, the conformity determination, and the IA currency basis in the maintenance record so the approval is auditable.

## 6. Major alteration versus major repair; what the IA does not reach

- Major alteration and major repair are treated in the same clause of 65.95(a)(1) and in the same renewal-credit option of 65.93(a)(2). The substantive difference is definitional (Appendix A to Part 43 addresses major alterations) and record-keeping (Appendix B to Part 43), not a difference in IA qualification.
- The IA does not authorize accomplishment of the alteration itself; accomplishment is a mechanic function. The IA function is inspection and approval for return to service.
- The IA cannot cure absent approved data: an alteration done on unapproved data is not made approvable by the IA holding the authorization.
- The IA privilege does not extend to Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft for major repair/alteration approval.
- The fixed base of operations under 65.91(c)(3) does not confine where the authority is exercised; the rule says so expressly.

## 7. Prerated arithmetic for the 90-day rate options (illustrative only)

65.93(a)(1) and (a)(2) state rates, not fixed totals: 'for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority.' A full 2-year cycle is about 730 days; 730 / 90 = 8.11 ninety-day units.

| Option | Rate | Prerated minimum for a full 730-day cycle | Check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 65.93(a)(1) | 1 annual inspection / 90 days | at least 9 | 9 ≥ 8.11 ✓ (8 would be 8.0 < 8.11 and is insufficient) |
| 65.93(a)(2) | 2 major repairs or major alterations / 90 days | at least 17 | 2 × 8.11 = 16.2; 17 ≥ 16.2 ✓ (16 would be below the rate and is insufficient) |

These figures are prorated illustrations for planning; the regulatory obligation is the rate itself, and partial periods must be counted conservatively against the days actually held. Do not cite 8 or 16 as satisfying a full 730-day cycle.

## 8. Verification, currency, and known gaps

- Currency. Text fetched 2026-11-15T03:45:08Z from the eCFR 'current' edition. Before any operational or training use, re-check the eCFR point-in-time currency for sections 65.91, 65.93 and 65.95 and confirm no intervening amendment.

Obtain these from the eCFR links before relying on completeness.

- Non-binding guidance: the FAA IA Information Guide (https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/2022-07/ia_info_guide.pdf) is informational and does not itself impose or relieve any requirement; where it diverges from the codified text, the codified text controls.
- Out of scope: military and foreign applicability, Part 129 operators, delegations (DAR/DER) as an alternative approval path, and Part 145 repair-station approval procedures.

question: IA
answer:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) and Major Alterations — 14 CFR Part 65, Subparts D and E

## 0. Short answer

There is no separate 'major alteration qualification' stacked on top of the IA. The qualification **is** the Inspection Authorization, and it has two distinct parts that the question conflates:

- **Track A — Eligibility to hold the IA at all** (14 CFR 65.91(c)). The written test that every IA applicant must pass is explicitly a test on inspection standards for *returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations*, so major-alteration competence is baked into the IA qualification itself.
- **Track B — The conditions under which an IA holder may act on a major alteration** (14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)). Holding the IA is necessary but not sufficient: the approval is limited to work done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator, and it excludes aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.

Governing code: **14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D (Inspection Authorization)** — specifically § 65.91 (eligibility), § 65.93 (renewal), § 65.95 (privileges and limitations).

---

## 1. Track A — Qualifications to obtain the IA

### 1.1 Verbatim rule text, 14 CFR § 65.91(c) (verified against eCFR)

> '(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must— (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years; (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter; (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority; (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.'
> — eCFR, 14 CFR 65.91(c)

### 1.2 The five qualifications, restated as a checklist

| # | Qualification | Regulatory hook | Notes for an AMT |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mechanic certificate with **both** Airframe and Powerplant ratings, currently effective, and **in effect for a total of at least 3 years** | 65.91(c)(1) | Airframe-only or Powerplant-only is disqualifying. The 3-year clock runs on the certificate/ratings, not on employment. |
| 2 | **Actively engaged for at least the 2 years before application** in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR Chapter I | 65.91(c)(2) | This is the experience element and it overlaps the 3-year certificate element but is not identical — you must show *activity*, not merely holding the certificate. |
| 3 | **Fixed base of operations** where reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week | 65.91(c)(3) | Need not be where the IA work is performed. |
| 4 | **Equipment, facilities, and inspection data** available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | 65.91(c)(4) | Practical capability element; current technical data is part of the requirement. |
| 5 | **Pass a written test** on ability to inspect to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | 65.91(c)(5) | This is the direct textual link between the IA qualification and major alterations. |

**Application mechanics.** Section 65.91(a)–(b) addresses how application is made (form and manner prescribed by the Administrator) and entitlement upon meeting the section. *Verification status: not quoted in the fetched material; confirm the current text at the eCFR page before relying on it in a written procedure.*

### 1.3 Currency / renewal — 14 CFR § 65.93

Verbatim (verified):

> '(a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, to be eligible for renewal of an inspection authorization for a 2-year period an applicant must present evidence during the month of March of each odd-numbered year, at the responsible Flight Standards office, that the applicant still meets the requirements of § 65.91(c)(1) through (4).'

Summary of the remaining renewal element (from the research record, not quoted verbatim): during the period the applicant held the IA, the applicant must also show qualifying recent activity — the recorded example being **at least two major repairs or major alterations, or both, for each 90 days of current authority** (or the equivalent annual/progressive-inspection activity set out in the same paragraph).

> **Verification flag:** the exact activity list and rate in 65.93(a)(1) should be read off the current eCFR text before it is used as an audit criterion. Treat the '2 per 90 days' figure as the regulation's stated rate, not as a number to be multiplied into a total for a 2-year cycle — the rule is written as a rate, and any derived total would be the engineer's arithmetic rather than the rule.

Key point for the question asked: renewal re-tests only 65.91(c)(1)–(4) plus activity — it does not re-administer the (c)(5) written test.

---

## 2. Track B — What the IA actually authorizes on a major alteration

### 2.1 Verbatim rule text, 14 CFR § 65.95 (verified against eCFR)

> '(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may— (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.'

> '(b) When he exercises the authority of this section, the holder of an inspection authorization shall endorse the aircraft logbook or other permanent record with his signature, the certificate number, and the kind of certificate held.'

### 2.2 Decomposed into the four conditions an IA must satisfy before signing

Every one of these must hold; failure of any one removes the authority for that item:

1. **The work is a major alteration** (as opposed to minor). Determined by the 14 CFR 1.1 definition, the Part 43 Appendix A list, and 21.93's major-change standard — see § 3 below.
2. **The work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.** The IA does not create or 'bless' data; the data must already be FAA-approved. Typical approved-data routes: type certificate / STC data, data approved under a PMA or TSO authorization, and FAA field-approved data executed on the FAA Form 337. Advisory material: AC 43-210A (Standardized Procedures for Requesting Approval of Data for Major Repairs and Major Alterations) and AC 21-40A.
3. **The aircraft is not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.** The parenthetical in 65.95(a)(1) is an express carve-out. (Part 121 operators use their own approved continuous airworthiness maintenance programs and authorized persons.)
4. **The alteration was performed by a person or entity authorized to perform it** (Part 43 performance rules — see § 4). The IA's function is *inspection and approval for return to service*, not performance of the alteration.

### 2.3 The endorsement — 65.95(b)

The record entry must contain, at minimum: **signature**, **certificate number**, and **kind of certificate held**. An approval that omits any of the three is defective on its face.

---

## 3. Threshold question: is it a major alteration?

The IA authority only engages if the item is major. Two regulatory anchors plus guidance:

- **14 CFR 21.93 (verbatim, verified):** "A 'minor change' is one that has no appreciable effect on the weight, balance, structural strength, reliability, operational characteristics, or other characteristics affecting the airworthiness of the product. All other changes are 'major changes' (except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section)."
- **14 CFR 1.1 / FAA guidance (verbatim from AC 120-77B):** "Major Alteration. An alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications. 1. An alteration that might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or 2. An alteration that is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations (refer to 14 CFR § 1.1)."
- **14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A** contains the enumerated lists of major alterations (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance) and major repairs, plus the preventive-maintenance list. Use Appendix A first; if the item is not listed, apply the appreciable-effect test.

*Verification flag: the Appendix A cross-reference is cited for context and was not fetched; confirm paragraph lettering against current eCFR before quoting it in a procedure.*

---

## 4. Surrounding Part 43 obligations that condition the IA's approval

These are cross-references, not part of the fetched verbatim set; confirm exact paragraph text at eCFR before use in a compliance document.

- **43.3 / 43.7** — who may perform alterations; a mechanic may perform alteration work for which he or she is rated.
- **43.5** — approval for return to service requires, among other things, that the 43.9 record entry be made, that any required FAA repair/alteration form be executed, and that any resulting change to operating limitations or approved flight manual data be incorporated.
- **43.9** — maintenance record entries; major repairs/alterations drive the FAA Form 337 (Major Repair and Alteration) requirement.
- **43.13** — work must be done using the methods, techniques, and practices prescribed in the current manufacturer's maintenance manual or Instructions for Continued Airworthiness, or other methods acceptable to the FAA.
- **91.417** — operator recordkeeping, including retention of major alteration records and Form 337 copies for aircraft operated under Part 91.

---

## 5. What the IA qualification does **not** confer (common misconceptions)

1. **It is not a data-approval authority.** An IA cannot approve the *technical data*; the data must already be approved by the Administrator. (Field approvals are an FAA/designee function, not an IA privilege.)
2. **It is not available on Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft** for major repair/alteration return to service — express carve-out in 65.95(a)(1).
3. **It is not a performance authority.** It is an inspection-and-return-to-service authority layered on the mechanic certificate; the alteration itself must be performed by an appropriately rated person or repair station under Part 43.
4. **It is not a substitute for the underlying ratings.** The IA sits on top of the A&P certificate; scope of work remains bounded by the mechanic certificate held (see 65.81(a) rating limitation) and by the IA holder's capability under 65.91(c)(4).
5. **It is not delegable.** 65.95(a) confers the privilege on 'the holder'; the approval and the 65.95(b) endorsement are personal acts.
6. **It is not an airworthiness-certificate authority.** Issuance of standard airworthiness certificates is a separate function.

---

## 6. Practical pre-signature checklist for an IA on a major alteration

1. Confirm the item is major — Part 43 Appendix A list, then 21.93 / 1.1 appreciable-effect test.
2. Confirm the aircraft is not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
3. Obtain and read the **FAA-approved technical data** that the alteration was performed to; verify revision/effectivity against the specific aircraft, engine, or propeller serial number.
4. Verify the alteration was performed by an authorized person/entity (43.3, 43.7) and that workmanship and methods conform to 43.13.
5. Perform the inspection yourself against that approved data; document the scope of inspection.
6. Confirm weight-and-balance and operating-limitation/approved-flight-manual impacts are addressed (43.5(a)(3)).
7. Confirm the maintenance record entry (43.9) and the FAA Form 337 are properly executed, including the approved-data basis.
8. Endorse the aircraft logbook or other permanent record with **signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate held** (65.95(b)).
9. Retain/route records per 91.417 (or the applicable operating rule).

---

## 8. Assumptions and what would change this answer

- Assumed **U.S. 14 CFR** applies and that 'FAA-AMT' means an Aviation Maintenance Technician certificated under Part 65 — not a Part 147 school, not a foreign authority.
- Assumed **'qualifications' means regulatory eligibility, currency, and the conditions on exercising the privilege**, not employer, union, or repair-station policy.
- Assumed **'major alterations'** carries the regulatory meaning (Part 43 Appendix A / 1.1 / 21.93), not a colloquial 'big job.'
- Assumed the **current eCFR edition** as of the fetch date. Part 65 text is stable but the reader should re-pull the section for the effective date of any specific approval.
- If the intent was instead the **repair station** side (Part 145, 145.213 inspection of work, or a Part 145 IA-equivalent), or the **Part 121 operator** side (continuous airworthiness program, 121.367/121.369), the answer changes materially — those are separate authorization regimes.
- If the intent was **FAA Form 337 field-approval procedure** rather than IA qualification, the governing guidance is AC 43-210A, not Part 65.
